USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold our negotiating posture through the March 1 deadline rather than escalating or conceding. Keep the credible threat of raising List 3 tariffs to 25% on the table as our principal leverage, continue the Washington talks toward a written memorandum of understanding, and only extend the deadline in exchange for concrete, enforceable commitments on IP protection, forced technology transfer, and an enforcement mechanism. Do not pull the tariff trigger now at a fragile moment in the US recovery, but equally do not roll back tariffs before we lock in enforcement.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is modest but real, so I rate it +0.2 rather than an opportunity. We hold the initiative — tariffs already cover ~$250B of Chinese imports and China has shown it is under pressure (soybean purchase commitments, yuan support/inflation 6.88 to 6.74 defusing the currency trigger, pledges of WTO-compliant subsidies and a 'consensus in principle' per Xinhua). But the US economy is softening and would be hurt by over-escalation: the 10-yr yield has fallen from ~3.2% in October to 2.65%, industrial production slipped from 103.4 to 102.8, and consumer sentiment (91.2 Jan) is still below its autumn level — so a 25% tariff jump risks markets and adds recession drag (timeline web_search: Reuters/CNBC on the hard March 1 deadline and 'stalemate on the important stuff'). This justifies a balanced action stance at 0.0: negotiate. Escalating to 25% on a fragile economy could backfire on US consumers, farmers, and allies (and strengthen the case for China's 'unfair US' narrative), while a premature full rollback would squander leverage before enforceable commitments — enforcement is precisely the unresolved 'hard deadline' core Lighthizer stressed (web_search/Reuters). Hold the tariff threat as leverage, negotiate the MOU, and extend only for tangible, verifiable progress.
